title: WHAT IF I SECRETLY ENJOY MY SIN?
paragraphs: WHAT IF I SECRETLY ENJOY MY SIN?

The terrifying question isn’t only, “Why do I keep falling?” Sometimes it’s, “What if part of me doesn’t actually want to stop?” And that may be exactly where Jesus wants to meet you—not to excuse what is destroying you, but to bring into the light what you have been afraid to admit.
There is a confession Christians know how to make.
“I sinned.”
There is another confession that is much harder.
“I sinned again.”
But there is one confession so uncomfortable that many believers would rather bury it beneath worship songs, church attendance, Bible verses, ministry activity, and carefully edited testimonies.
“I think part of me enjoyed it.”
There.
That sentence.
The one you hoped nobody would say out loud.
Because what happens when you aren’t only fighting something you hate?
What happens when part of you still wants it?
What happens when you prayed for deliverance in the morning…and quietly missed the temptation by evening?

What happens when you deleted it, blocked it, confessed it, cried about it, promised God you were finished with it—and then somewhere deep inside yourself felt disappointed when the opportunity disappeared?
What if you love Jesus…
but there is still something in the darkness that you enjoy?
Keep reading.
Because pretending that sin has no pleasure will never help you understand why you keep returning to it.
The Bible is far more honest than that.
Hebrews speaks of Moses refusing to remain identified with Pharaoh’s household, choosing instead to suffer with God’s people rather than enjoy what Scripture calls the temporary pleasure of sin.
The Greek phrase in Hebrews 11:25 is devastatingly honest:
“πρόσκαιρον ἔχειν ἁμαρτίας ἀπόλαυσιν”
It speaks of having the enjoyment or pleasure of sin for a season.
That word “πρόσκαιρον” carries the idea of something temporary, something lasting only for a time.
Scripture does not need to lie about sin to defeat sin.
Sin can feel good.
For a season.
That is part of what makes it dangerous.

If sin were always immediately miserable, temptation would hardly require resistance. If adultery tasted like ashes before the first touch, if pornography produced loneliness before the first image, if gossip destroyed friendships before the first sentence, if drunkenness delivered the hangover before the intoxication, if revenge wounded us before satisfying our anger, and if pride humiliated us before making us feel important, temptation would lose much of its power.
But sin frequently puts pleasure at the entrance…
and hides death farther down the road.
James describes the progression with frightening precision:
“Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death” (James 1:14–15).
Notice where James begins.
Desire.
Not merely demons.
Not merely circumstances.
Not merely bad friends.
Not merely algorithms.
Not merely culture.
Something inside us can respond to temptation.
And Jesus Himself said something equally uncomfortable:
“And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil” (John 3:19).
Loved the darkness.
That is stronger than accidentally wandering into it.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading this needs to stop pretending.
Maybe you have been asking God to remove a sin while secretly keeping a chair for it in your heart.
Maybe you hate what pornography does to your soul but still crave what it makes you feel.
Maybe you hate your bitterness but enjoy replaying what they did because anger allows you to punish them inside your imagination.
Maybe you hate gossip until the conversation becomes interesting.
Maybe you condemn sexual immorality publicly while entertaining fantasies privately.
Maybe you say you want freedom from alcohol, substances, attention, validation, lust, envy, greed, rage, or an unhealthy relationship—but there are moments when you miss the escape.
Maybe your sin gives you something.
Comfort.
Control.
Pleasure.
Attention.
Numbness.
Power.
Revenge.
Fantasy.
Belonging.
Relief.
For a few minutes, it quiets something hurting inside you.
Then the pleasure leaves.
And the chains remain.
This is why simply saying, “Sin is bad,” sometimes feels insufficient when temptation comes screaming.
Your heart already knows sin is bad.
The deeper question is:
What have you been asking sin to give you that you were created to seek ultimately in God?
That question can hurt.
But sometimes grace begins where pretending ends.
David understood something profound after his catastrophic sin involving Bathsheba and Uriah. When his hidden corruption was exposed, he did not merely ask God to improve his public behavior.
He prayed:
“לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים”
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10).
David understood that he needed more than reputation repair.
More than consequences removed.
More than behavioral management.
He needed God to work at the level of the heart.
And look carefully at the Hebrew verb translated “create”:
“בְּרָא” — bara.
It is the same foundational Hebrew verb used in Genesis 1:1 when Scripture declares that God “created” the heavens and the earth.
David was essentially throwing himself upon the creative power of God.
God…
there is something wrong inside me that I cannot merely polish.
Create cleanliness where corruption has lived.
Do something in me that I cannot manufacture by pretending harder.
And perhaps that is your prayer too.
Because there is an enormous difference between being tempted by sin, struggling against sin, falling into sin, and finally making peace with sin.
A Christian may experience horrifying temptation.
A Christian may stumble grievously.
A Christian may find himself echoing Paul’s anguish in Romans 7, bewildered by the contradiction between what he knows is right and what he finds himself doing.
But grace never teaches us to rename darkness as light.
Grace does not say, “Since Jesus forgives you, enjoy your chains.”
Paul confronts that distortion directly:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” (Romans 6:1–2).
Grace is not permission to remain comfortably imprisoned.
Grace opens the prison door.
And this matters enormously:
The fact that temptation feels pleasurable does not automatically prove that you do not love Christ.
Temptation would scarcely be temptation if nothing about it appealed to you.
The question is not merely whether your flesh can feel an attraction toward sin.
The deeper question is what you do with that attraction.
Do you feed it?
Defend it?
Plan for it?
Hide it?
Rename it?
Make excuses for it?
Or do you drag it trembling into the presence of Christ and say:
“Jesus, this is what I actually want sometimes. I hate admitting it. Change what I love.”
That may be one of the most honest prayers you have ever prayed.
Not:
“Lord, I would never want this.”
But:
“Lord, sometimes I do want this, and that frightens me. Please transform my desires.”
That is not permission for sin.
That is war.
Repentance is deeper than feeling disgusting after you fail.
Biblical repentance involves a turning—a changed posture toward sin and toward God.
You can feel terrible about consequences without truly repenting.
Judas felt crushing remorse.
Pharaoh regretted consequences.
People can hate what sin costs while continuing to love what sin offers.
Repentance goes deeper.
It says:
“I have been treating poison like medicine.”
It stops negotiating.
It stops calling bondage “just how I am.”
It stops asking how close to the edge it can stand without technically falling.
It begins asking a different question:
“How close can I walk with Jesus?”
And that change does not mean the battle instantly disappears.
Sometimes repentance begins while desire is still screaming.
You may genuinely turn toward Christ while part of your flesh is still begging you to turn around.
This is why Christian holiness cannot be reduced to willpower.
God promised something much deeper:
“And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).
Christianity is not God finding morally impressive people and rewarding them.
The Gospel is God rescuing sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
Jesus did not go to the cross because your sin was a minor personality defect.
He went because sin brings guilt, slavery, alienation, judgment, and death.
And the cross tells us two truths simultaneously:
Your sin is more serious than your excuses have admitted.
And the mercy of Christ is greater than your shame has imagined.
Look at Jesus.
Betrayed.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
The sin we sometimes pet in secret is the very rebellion for which the spotless Son of God gave Himself.
Yet He did not remain in the grave.
Christ rose.
And because He rose, the Gospel is not merely an announcement that guilty people can be forgiven.
It is the announcement that dead people can receive life.
Slaves can become free.
Enemies can become children.
The ashamed can come home.
The unclean can be washed.
The condemned who are in Christ can stand under the astonishing declaration of Romans 8:1:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation does not mean no transformation.
The Christ who forgives you also claims you.
The Savior who washes you also calls you to follow Him.
Jesus does not rescue us so we can crawl lovingly back toward the chains He broke.
He calls us into life.
So what if you secretly enjoy your sin?
Tell Him.
Not because He does not already know.
Because you need to stop hiding.
Tell Jesus the ugly version.
Tell Him without Christian vocabulary designed to make your darkness sound respectable.
“Jesus, I like the attention.”
“Jesus, I enjoy the fantasy.”
“Jesus, I want revenge.”
“Jesus, I like being desired.”
“Jesus, I enjoy getting drunk.”
“Jesus, I like feeling superior.”
“Jesus, I keep returning to that screen because for a moment I do not feel lonely.”
“Jesus, I know this relationship dishonors You, but I am afraid of being alone.”
“Jesus, I know I should forgive, but part of me enjoys hating them.”
“Jesus, I want You…
but sometimes I want this too.”
Then ask Him for something greater than stronger self-control.
Ask Him for transformed affection.
Ask Him to become more beautiful to you than the thing competing for your worship.
Because the deepest victory is not merely saying no while staring longingly at Egypt.
It is discovering that Christ is better.
Better than lust.
Better than revenge.
Better than applause.
Better than intoxication.
Better than secret fantasies.
Better than money.
Better than being wanted by somebody who pulls you away from God.
Better than the temporary pleasure that leaves you emptier than it found you.
And when you fall, do not turn repentance into another form of self-worship by spending days obsessing over how horrible you are.
Run to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Then get serious about the pathways that repeatedly carry you toward sin.

Bring darkness into accountable Christian community. Seek mature pastoral help where appropriate. Remove access where wisdom requires it. Stop protecting environments that continually feed temptation. Saturate your mind with Scripture. Pray when you do not feel spiritual. Worship when your emotions lag behind obedience.
And remember this:
You are not saved because you finally become impressive enough for Jesus.
You are saved by grace through faith in Christ.
But the grace that saves does not leave sin enthroned without a fight.
“For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:14).
Maybe you have spent years asking:
“How could God love me after what I did?”
Look at the cross.
Maybe you have spent years asking:
“Can Jesus really forgive this?”
Look at the cross.
Maybe your question tonight is even darker:
“What if I knowingly went back because I wanted it?”
Look at the cross…
and repent.
Do not use grace as camouflage.
Use grace as your reason to come home.
Peter denied Jesus after insisting he never would.
Three times.
The scandal was real.
The failure was public.
The shame must have been unbearable.
Yet Jesus met Peter after the resurrection.
He restored him.
He recommissioned him.
Peter's worst chapter did not receive permission to become his final chapter.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin harmless.
Not by changing God's standard until rebellion becomes comfortable.
Jesus rewrites everything by entering the wreckage with wounds in His hands, paying the sinner's debt, defeating death, forgiving the repentant, restoring the fallen, and making people new.
Maybe your scandal has never become public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your friends do not know.
The people who see your Bible posts do not know.
But Jesus knows.
And still He calls sinners to come into the light.
Do not wait until sin destroys enough of your life to become disgusting.
Do not wait until the pleasure stops being pleasurable.
Do not wait until somebody discovers you.
Come now.
While your heart is still beating.
While conviction is still speaking.
While the door of repentance stands open.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But you can stop pretending.
Maybe someone reading the comments needs to discover that they are not the only Christian fighting a battle they are ashamed to admit.
And if you know somebody quietly losing a war with temptation, do not send this article as an accusation.
Send it as a lifeline.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
Christ alone saves, and we glorify God through lives surrendered to Him.
And there is something else we want believers to know.
Leave thinking about Christ.
Because one day your secret sin will not matter because somebody wrote an emotionally powerful article about it.
It will matter because sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Eternity is real.
But so is the cross.
So is the empty tomb.
So is forgiveness.
So is grace.
So is the blood of Jesus Christ that cleanses sinners.
So is the Spirit of God who transforms hearts.
So is the Savior who still receives people willing to stop hiding and come home.
You may have enjoyed the sin.
You may even miss it tomorrow.
But you do not have to worship what once enslaved you.
Bring the desire itself to Jesus.
Bring the appetite.
Bring the fantasy.
Bring the relapse.
Bring the shame.
Bring the part of yourself you desperately wish were not there.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Walk in the light.
And when temptation whispers, “You still want me,” you can answer with something greater than denial:
“Maybe my flesh remembers you.
But I belong to Jesus now.”
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become evidence that Christians do not have to pretend they have never bled in battle.
Because perhaps the most dangerous lie your secret sin ever told you was not, “This will satisfy you.”
Perhaps it was:
“After enjoying this, Jesus could never want you back.”
The cross says otherwise.
Your sin may remember your name, but it does not get to write your ending—Jesus does.
